item.title: Pacific Islands
item.description: Pacific nations are pushing for stronger regional cooperation and sustainable early warning systems as climate-related hazards continue to threaten communities across the region. The issues were highlighted at the Eighth Meeting of the Pacific Meteorological Council was officially opened at the Fa'onelua centre in Nuku'alofa today.
item.content:encoded:
Pacific nations are pushing for stronger regional cooperation and sustainable early warning systems as climate-related hazards continue to threaten communities across the region.

The issues were highlighted at the Eighth Meeting of the Pacific Meteorological Council was officially opened at the Fa'onelua centre in Nuku'alofa today.

Delivering the keynote address, Dr Viliami Latu said Pacific countries needed to ensure investments in meteorological and disaster infrastructure could be maintained long after development projects ended. He asked delegates to consider who would maintain weather and early warning systems five, 10 and 20 years after the projects that funded them had ended.

“An early warning system that cannot be maintained will eventually cease to be an early warning system,” he said.

Dr Latu said maintenance, replacement, insurance, lifecycle costs, national capacity and sustainable financing needed to be considered from the beginning of every investment.

“This is not simply a technical issue, it is a question of Pacific resilience, development and security.”

World Meteorological Organization Regional Office Director Ishaam Abader said strengthening meteorological services was ultimately about protecting Pacific communities.

“Strengthening weather, climate and water services is not only about science and technology,” Abader said.

“It is more importantly about protecting lives, supporting sustainable development, safeguarding livelihoods and enhancing resilience across Pacific communities.”

Dr Latu said future partnerships with development partners must ensure systems built with external support could eventually be operated, maintained and sustained by Pacific nations.

He said new satellite technology, forecasting systems and artificial intelligence would strengthen meteorological services, but technology alone would not make the Pacific “Weather Ready”.

“The most important investment we can make remains an investment in our people,” he said.

Dr Latu highlighted the role of meteorologists, hydrologists, technicians, observers, forecasters, disaster managers, communicators and communities in building resilience.

He also stressed regional cooperation, saying weather systems and natural hazards did not recognise national borders.

Pacific nations needed to continue sharing knowledge, observations, technology, expertise and resources while developing systems that reflected regional priorities, he said.

Dr Latu said the Pacific Meteorological Council provided an important platform for that collective work.

He challenged delegates to consider whether decisions made at the meeting would ultimately make Pacific communities safer.

“If the answer is yes, then our work is worthwhile,” he said.

Dr Latu said Pacific communities could combine traditional knowledge of the environment with modern science and technology to better understand and respond to hazards.

He said the goal should be a Pacific where communities understood the risks they faced, received warnings in time and could act before hazards became tragedies.

“That is the Pacific we should seek to build,” he said.

“A Pacific that is informed. A Pacific that is prepared. A Pacific whose systems are sustainable. And ultimately, a Pacific that is ‘Secure’.”
